items.question: In evaluating a concrete trapezoidal lateral canal, what should be the thickness of the reinforced wall?
items.rationale: Under standard NIA/PAES irrigation canal design specifications, reinforced concrete walls for trapezoidal lateral canals require a minimum thickness of 15 cm to withstand earth and hydrostatic loads.

choiceExplanations.15 cm: Correct — Standard NIA/PAES design specifications require a 15 cm reinforced concrete wall thickness for lateral irrigation canals to resist cracking and earth pressure.
choiceExplanations.20 cm: A 20 cm wall thickness is generally reserved for larger main canals or high-load structures rather than standard laterals.
choiceExplanations.10 cm: A 10 cm lining is typical for small unreinforced farm ditches and is too thin for reinforced lateral canals.
choiceExplanations.25 cm: A 25 cm wall thickness is over-designed and uneconomical for standard lateral irrigation canals.

items.question: A farm needs to pasteurize 500 kg of milk from 25 °C to 72 °C. The specific heat of milk is 3.9 kJ/kg·°C. Calculate the energy required.

choiceExplanations.85.65 MJ: An energy of 85.65 MJ underestimates the sensible heat needed for a 47 °C temperature rise.
choiceExplanations.91.65 MJ: Correct — Sensible heat required is Q = mcΔT = 500 kg × 3.9 kJ/(kg·°C) × (72 − 25)°C = 91,650 kJ = 91.65 MJ.
choiceExplanations.90.65 MJ: An energy of 90.65 MJ falls 1 MJ short of the exact mcΔT calculation.
choiceExplanations.80.65 MJ: An energy of 80.65 MJ corresponds to only about a 41.4 °C temperature rise instead of 47 °C.

items.question: In evaluating specific conditions that necessitate the provision of a canal fall, which one is not to be considered?
items.rationale: Canal falls are installed to address excessive ground slope, avoid high embankments, or cross drainage channels, and they rely on energy dissipation rather than energy conservation.

choiceExplanations.Crossing Drainage Channels: Crossing natural drainage channels can require adjusting canal grade or elevation, making fall placement relevant.
choiceExplanations.Avoiding High Embankments: Canal falls help keep the canal bed close to ground level, avoiding costly high embankments.
choiceExplanations.Excessive ground slope: When natural terrain slopes more steeply than the canal design slope, canal falls prevent erosive velocities.
choiceExplanations.Energy conservation: Correct — Canal falls deliberately dissipate excess hydraulic energy rather than conserving it, so energy conservation is not a design reason for providing one.

items.question: Evaluate and select the most appropriate criteria for designing an unlined trapezoidal open channel.
items.rationale: The standard hydraulic design criterion for an unlined trapezoidal open channel is the best hydraulic cross-section, which minimizes wetted perimeter for a given flow area to maximize flow efficiency and reduce excavation and seepage.

choiceExplanations.Most efficient canal: Informal label not used as the standard design criterion for unlined trapezoidal channels.
choiceExplanations.Moderately efficient canal: Non-standard term that does not define optimal hydraulic geometry for channel design.
choiceExplanations.Best hydraulic cross-section: Correct — The best hydraulic cross-section minimizes wetted perimeter for a given flow area, reducing excavation and friction losses.
choiceExplanations.Good hydraulic cross-section: General descriptive phrase rather than the formal hydraulic optimization criterion.

items.question: Find the area bounded by the curve y = 9 - x², x = -2, x = 2, and the x-axis.
items.rationale: Integrating y = 9 - x² from x = -2 to x = 2 yields 2 × [9x - x³/3] from 0 to 2 = 2 × (18 - 8/3) = 92/3 square units.

choiceExplanations.31/4: Incorrect value; 31/4 equals 7.75, far below the definite integral under the parabola.
choiceExplanations.31/3: Incorrect value; 31/3 equals 10.33, whereas the curve reaches y = 9 at x = 0.
choiceExplanations.92/4: Incorrect value; 92/4 equals 23, which misapplies the denominator of the x³/3 antiderivative.
choiceExplanations.92/3: Correct — Integrating 9 − x² from −2 to 2 gives 2[9(2) − 2³/3] = 2(46/3) = 92/3.

items.question: dam composed of a single kind of embankment material exclusive for slope protection

choiceExplanations.Composite embankment: Embankment combining multiple distinct material sections or combining earthfill with a concrete or rock section.
choiceExplanations.Diaphragm embankment: Embankment featuring a thin vertical impervious membrane or cutoff wall inside a pervious shell.
choiceExplanations.Zoned embankment: Embankment built with a central impervious core flanked by outer shells of more pervious materials.
choiceExplanations.Homogenous embankment: Correct — A homogeneous embankment uses a single uniform soil material throughout, excluding outer slope protection layers.

items.question: vertical flow of water to below the root zone which is affected by soil structure, texture, bulk density, mineralogy, organic matter content, salt type and concentration
items.source: Area 2 IRRIGATION STRUCTURES; Tambong Subject B Part 2; area 2 TERMINOLOGIES

choiceExplanations.Interflow: Lateral subsurface movement of water above a less permeable layer before reaching a stream.
choiceExplanations.Percolation: Correct — Percolation is the downward vertical movement of water through saturated or near-saturated soil below the root zone.
choiceExplanations.Seepage: Slow lateral or downward flow of water through porous embankments, dam foundations, or canal banks.
choiceExplanations.Infiltration: Initial entry of surface water downward into the soil surface rather than movement below the root zone.

items.question: dam consisting a central impervious core flanked between zones of more pervious materials

choiceExplanations.Rockfill embankment: Embankment constructed primarily of dumped or compacted rock with an upstream facing or core for watertightness.
choiceExplanations.Homogenous embankment: Embankment built from a single uniform soil type throughout rather than distinct pervious and impervious zones.
choiceExplanations.Diaphragm embankment: Embankment containing a thin artificial membrane or cutoff wall rather than a broad earth core.
choiceExplanations.Zoned embankment: Correct — A zoned embankment places a central low-permeability clay core between outer stabilizing shells of pervious sand or gravel.

items.question: Water is impounded against the slope behind a semicircular embankment.

choiceExplanations.Straight embankment: Linear embankment built straight across a depression or valley rather than curving around a hillside.
choiceExplanations.Semi circular embankment: Correct — A semicircular embankment curves around a hillside slope to impound surface runoff behind a curved earth bund.
choiceExplanations.L-shaped embankment: Two-legged embankment bent roughly 90 degrees to trap runoff at a slope corner.
choiceExplanations.Dugout embankment: Excavated below-grade pit pond dug into flat ground rather than impounding water against a hillslope.

items.question: internal erosion induced by regressive erosion of particles from downstream and along the upstream line towards an outside environment

choiceExplanations.Scouring: Surface erosion and removal of soil or rock particles by fast-flowing open-channel water.
choiceExplanations.Sloughing: Localized surface sliding or caving of a saturated downstream embankment slope rather than internal tunnel erosion.
choiceExplanations.Piping: Correct — Piping is backward internal erosion where seepage detaches soil particles from downstream toward upstream, forming open conduits.
choiceExplanations.Heaving: Upward boiling or lifting of soil at the downstream toe caused by excessive upward seepage pressure.

items.question: A type of terrace more common for mechanized farming systems on moderate slopes of 6 to 8 percent

choiceExplanations.Steep-backslope narrowbase terrace: Narrow-base terrace with an uncropped steep backslope, suited for steeper slopes rather than wide machinery.
choiceExplanations.Three-segment section broadbase: Correct — A three-segment broadbase terrace has wide, gently sloped front, back, and channel faces suited for mechanization on 6–8% slopes.
choiceExplanations.Conservation bench terrace: Wide flat bench cut into mild slopes to store runoff for moisture conservation in dryland farming.
choiceExplanations.Level-channel broadbase terrace: Flat-grade broadbase terrace with zero longitudinal channel slope, used mainly on permeable soils in low-rainfall areas.

items.question: Soil moisture tension with 15 atmospheres

choiceExplanations.Field capacity: Soil moisture content after free gravitational drainage stops, typically around 1/10 to 1/3 atmosphere tension.
choiceExplanations.Saturation point: Condition where all soil pores are completely filled with water at zero matric tension.
choiceExplanations.Hygroscopic coefficient: Thin water film adsorbed tightly to soil particles at roughly 31 atmospheres, unavailable to plants.
choiceExplanations.Permanent wilting point: Correct — Permanent wilting point occurs near 15 atmospheres of tension, beyond which most plants cannot extract water and recover.

items.question: What is the term for the soil moisture content remaining after gravitational water has drained away?

choiceExplanations.Permanent Wilting Point: Lower limit of available soil moisture at ~15 atm where plants wilt irreversibly.
choiceExplanations.Hygroscopic Coefficient: Tightly adsorbed moisture film around soil particles held near 31 atm tension.
choiceExplanations.Field Capacity: Correct — Field capacity is the upper limit of available water retained in soil pores after excess gravitational water drains away.
choiceExplanations.Saturation Capacity: Maximum water content when every soil pore space is completely filled with water.

items.question: Is the practice of growing different crops in alternate strips across the slope to serve as barriers for soil erosion?

choiceExplanations.Contour farming: Tilling and planting along contour lines across a slope without necessarily alternating distinct crop bands.
choiceExplanations.Strip cropping: Correct — Strip cropping alternates strips of row crops and close-growing crops across slopes to slow runoff and trap eroded soil.
choiceExplanations.Mulch tillage: Leaving crop residues on the soil surface during tillage to cushion raindrop impact and reduce runoff.
choiceExplanations.Cover cropping: Planting a dense protective crop over an entire field primarily to shield bare soil between main crops.

items.question: Moisture content of the soil when gravitational water has been removed
items.source: RECALLED COMPRESS; Tambong Subject B Part 1

choiceExplanations.Field capacity: Correct — Field capacity is the moisture held by capillary forces in soil after gravitational water has drained out.
choiceExplanations.Saturation capacity: Total water content when all soil voids are completely filled with water.
choiceExplanations.Hygroscopic coefficient: Adsorbed vapor-like moisture film held at ~31 atm that is unavailable to plant roots.
choiceExplanations.Permanent wilting point: Lower moisture limit near 15 atm tension at which plants permanently wilt.

items.question: Erosion control management where in close growing crops in the same field oriented across the slope

choiceExplanations.Contour Farming: Correct — Contour farming orients tillage and close-growing crop rows along terrain contours across the slope to retard runoff.
choiceExplanations.Strip Cropping: Alternating bands of different crops across a slope to intercept runoff between strips.
choiceExplanations.Cover Cropping: Growing a protective canopy crop mainly to shield soil during fallow or between orchard rows.
choiceExplanations.Terrace Farming: Constructing physical earth embankments and channels across steep slopes to break slope length.

items.question: In Small Farm Reservoir, what is the maximum height of earth embankment

choiceExplanations.5m Pond area - 1350 m²: Understates the standard 1,500 m² maximum pond area specified for Small Farm Reservoirs.
choiceExplanations.5m Pond area - 1500 m²: Correct — Under Philippine Small Farm Reservoir standards, maximum earth embankment height is 5 m and maximum pond area is 1,500 m².
choiceExplanations.5m Pond area - 1200 m²: Matches the minimum or smaller pond area rather than the 1,500 m² maximum SFR limit.
choiceExplanations.5m Pond area - 1650 m²: Exceeds the standard 1,500 m² maximum pond surface area for a Small Farm Reservoir.

items.question: top width in SFR
items.answer: The width of the crest (Bt) can range from 2m to 3m.
choices: The width of the crest (Bt) can range from 2m to 3m.

choiceExplanations.6m to 8m: Excessively wide crest typical of large earth dams rather than small farm reservoirs.
choiceExplanations.The width of the crest (Bt) can range fr: Correct — For Small Farm Reservoirs, the embankment crest width (Bt) is specified at 2 m to 3 m.
choiceExplanations.1m to 1.5m: Too narrow for stable construction and safe compaction of an SFR earth embankment.
choiceExplanations.4m to 5m: Wider than required for standard Small Farm Reservoir earth embankments.

items.question: type of terracing with 6-8 % slope.

choiceExplanations.Narrow: Narrow-base terraces have steeper uncultivated ridges used on steeper slopes rather than 6–8% mechanized fields.
choiceExplanations.Zingg: Zingg terraces are conservation bench systems typically applied on steeper 9–24% slopes.
choiceExplanations.Bench: Bench terraces form stepped flat beds on steep hillsides generally exceeding 15–25% slope.
choiceExplanations.Broad: Correct — Broadbase terraces are designed for gentle to moderate 6–8% slopes where farm machinery crosses the terrace ridge.

items.question: SFR diversion channel depth

choiceExplanations.atleast 0.66m: Shallower than the 0.75 m minimum diversion channel depth required for Small Farm Reservoirs.
choiceExplanations.atleast 0.60m: Underestimates the standard 0.75 m minimum depth for SFR diversion channels.
choiceExplanations.atleast 0.75m: Correct — Small Farm Reservoir design guidelines require a diversion channel depth of at least 0.75 m to safely route runoff.
choiceExplanations.atleast 0.81m: Exceeds the standard 0.75 m minimum diversion channel depth requirement for SFRs.

items.question: SFR buffer strip

choiceExplanations.3–4m wide: Wider than the standard 1–2 m protective grassed buffer strip specified for SFRs.
choiceExplanations.1-2m wide: Correct — Standard Small Farm Reservoir layout specifies a 1–2 m wide vegetative buffer strip around the reservoir perimeter.
choiceExplanations.2–2m wide: Typographical range representing a fixed 2 m width rather than the standard 1–2 m specification.
choiceExplanations.2–3m wide: Exceeds the standard 1–2 m buffer strip width prescribed in SFR design criteria.

items.question: SFR Slope

choiceExplanations.0-15%: Correct — Small Farm Reservoirs are suited to flat to undulating terrain with slopes from 0% to 15%.
choiceExplanations.-15–0%: Invalid negative slope range that does not represent terrain gradient criteria for SFR siting.
choiceExplanations.15–30%: Too steep for standard SFR earth embankments, increasing embankment volume and instability risks.
choiceExplanations.30–45%: Very steep mountain terrain unsuitable for Small Farm Reservoir siting.

items.question: The primary purpose in limiting water flow not to go below minimum velocity.

choiceExplanations.Minimize seepage: Controlled primarily by lining materials and soil permeability rather than minimum flow velocity.
choiceExplanations.Prevent scouring: Prevented by limiting velocity below the maximum permissible non-erosive velocity, not the minimum velocity.
choiceExplanations.Avoid sedimentation: Correct — Maintaining flow above minimum non-silting velocity keeps suspended particles moving and prevents canal sedimentation.
choiceExplanations.Reduce evaporation: Depends on water surface area, wind, temperature, and humidity rather than minimum channel velocity.

items.question: The process by which the soil is removed from its natural place.

choiceExplanations.Soil leaching: Downward washing of dissolved nutrients and minerals through the soil profile by percolating water.
choiceExplanations.Soil subsidence: Downward settling or sinking of the ground surface due to compaction, drainage, or organic oxidation.
choiceExplanations.Soil weathering: In-situ physical and chemical breakdown of parent rock into soil without necessarily transporting particles away.
choiceExplanations.Soil erosion: Correct — Soil erosion is the detachment and transport of soil particles from their original location by water, wind, or gravity.

items.question: A kind of terrace which consists of a series of flattened areas.

choiceExplanations.Zingg terrace: Conservation terrace combining a sloped catchment with a flat leveled bench rather than a full stepped series.
choiceExplanations.Channel terrace: Drainage-type terrace built to intercept and carry surface runoff across moderate slopes rather than forming flat steps.
choiceExplanations.Broadbase terrace: Wide, gently sloped ridge-and-channel terrace farmable by machinery on moderate slopes.
choiceExplanations.Bench terrace: Correct — A bench terrace converts a steep hillside into a series of level or nearly level step-like flat strips for cultivation.

items.question: The simplest method of determining soil erosion over a period of time.

choiceExplanations.Tracer method: Uses radioactive or chemical isotopes to track sediment movement, requiring specialized laboratory equipment.
choiceExplanations.Plot method: Direct bounded runoff-plot collection measuring total soil loss, requiring substantial construction and maintenance.
choiceExplanations.Pin method: Correct — The erosion pin method drives calibrated stakes into soil to directly measure surface lowering or deposition over time.
choiceExplanations.Lysimeter method: Measures water percolation and evapotranspiration in an isolated soil column rather than surface soil loss.

items.question: Advanced form of erosion.

choiceExplanations.Sheet erosion: Uniform removal of thin soil layers over broad areas by overland flow; an early erosion stage.
choiceExplanations.Splash erosion: Initial detachment of soil particles caused directly by falling raindrops hitting bare ground.
choiceExplanations.Gully erosion: Correct — Gully erosion is an advanced stage where deep, wide channels form that cannot be erased by normal tillage.
choiceExplanations.Rill erosion: Intermediate erosion forming small, shallow channels that can still be smoothed out by regular plowing.

items.question: Dam consisting of stones enclosed in cyclone wires which allows water passage.

choiceExplanations.Gabion dam: Correct — gabions are wire-mesh baskets filled with stones; water seeps through the gaps while the structure checks erosion.
choiceExplanations.Rockfill dam: Wrong — a rockfill dam is dumped rock with an impervious core or face, not wire-caged stones.
choiceExplanations.Earthfill dam: Wrong — an earthfill dam is compacted soil built to hold water back, not pass it.
choiceExplanations.Masonry dam: Wrong — a masonry dam is stones bonded with mortar into a solid, watertight wall.

items.question: Philippine geographical constant for determining terrace vertical interval.

choiceExplanations.0.7: Too high for the standard Philippine constant used in the terrace vertical interval formula.
choiceExplanations.0.5: Correct — Philippine soil conservation standards use a geographical constant of 0.5 in calculating terrace vertical interval.
choiceExplanations.0.6: Exceeds the standard 0.5 Philippine geographical factor for terrace vertical interval spacing.
choiceExplanations.0.4: Underestimates the 0.5 Philippine constant used in terrace vertical interval design.

items.question: A trapezoidal concrete diversion dam has inclined upstream wall. Resisting moment relative to the dam toe is 263,953.2 tonne-meters while overturning moment is 96,233.3 tonne-meters per meter of dam width at deepest section. What is the safety factor against overturning? Is it safe?
items.answer: 2.74, safe Determining the Factor of Safety against Overturning, FSo FSo = RM/OM
items.rationale: 2.74, safe Determining the Factor of Safety against Overturning, FSo FSo = RM/OM / = 263,953.2/96,233.3 / = 2.74
choices: 2.74, safe Determining the Factor of Safety against Overturning, FSo FSo = RM/OM

choiceExplanations.1.74, unsafe: Incorrect ratio; 263,953.2 / 96,233.3 equals 2.74, not 1.74, and a ratio above 1.5 is safe.
choiceExplanations.2.36, safe: Incorrect division result; 263,953.2 divided by 96,233.3 gives 2.74 rather than 2.36.
choiceExplanations.0.36, unsafe: Incorrect inverted ratio (OM / RM ≈ 0.36) rather than resisting moment divided by overturning moment.
choiceExplanations.2.74, safe Determining the Factor of Saf: Correct — FSo = RM / OM = 263,953.2 / 96,233.3 = 2.74, which exceeds the minimum safety factor against overturning, making the dam safe.

items.question: Advanced stage of rill erosion. Rills when neglected develop in size and become ____.

choiceExplanations.Interrill erosion: Soil detachment and transport occurring between rills via raindrop splash and shallow sheet flow.
choiceExplanations.Gully erosion: Correct — Uncontrolled rills deepen and widen over time into gullies that normal tillage cannot remove.
choiceExplanations.Splash erosion: Initial particle detachment caused by raindrop impact before concentrated channel flow develops.
choiceExplanations.Sheet erosion: Uniform removal of thin topsoil layers by shallow overland flow rather than concentrated channels.

items.question: Combination of sheet and splash erosion

choiceExplanations.Streambank erosion: Scouring and collapse of stream or river channel sides caused by flowing water.
choiceExplanations.Rill erosion: Concentrated flow cutting small, tillage-erasable channels down a slope.
choiceExplanations.Gully erosion: Advanced erosion creating deep channels too large to cross with normal farm implements.
choiceExplanations.Interrill erosion: Correct — Interrill erosion combines raindrop splash detachment with shallow sheet flow transport between rills.

items.question: Primarily caused by raindrop

choiceExplanations.Gully erosion: Advanced concentrated channel erosion driven by heavy surface runoff rather than direct raindrop impact.
choiceExplanations.Splash/Raindrop erosion: Correct — Splash or raindrop erosion occurs when falling raindrops strike bare soil and scatter detached particles into the air.
choiceExplanations.Sheet erosion: Uniform removal of thin soil layers by shallow unchannelized overland flow.
choiceExplanations.Rill erosion: Formation of small, parallel micro-channels by concentrated surface runoff.

items.question: A type of terrace usually used for 9-24% slope characterized by breaking the slope at certain intervals by a ridge and a flat portion to trap runoff.

choiceExplanations.Broadbase terrace: Used on gentler slopes up to about 8% where farm equipment can cross the broad ridge.
choiceExplanations.Zingg terrace: Correct — A Zingg conservation bench terrace suits 9–24% slopes, using a ridge and flat leveled bench to impound runoff.
choiceExplanations.Bench terrace: Stepped hillside terrace system typically applied on steep slopes above 15–25%.
choiceExplanations.Channel terrace: Drainage terrace built mainly to convey excess runoff along a gentle grade rather than pond it on a flat bench.

items.question: Ratio of the bulk density of the soil with the density of water; it is the ratio of the weight of soil to the weight of water with volume equal to the total soil volume

choiceExplanations.Bulk density: Mass of dry soil per unit total bulk volume, expressed in dimensions of mass/volume rather than a dimensionless ratio.
choiceExplanations.Particle density: Mass of solid soil particles per unit volume of solids only, excluding pore space.
choiceExplanations.Apparent specific gravity: Correct — Apparent specific gravity is the dimensionless ratio of soil bulk density to water density, using total soil volume.
choiceExplanations.Real specific gravity: Ratio of particle density (solids volume only) to the density of water.

items.question: A crop grown between orchard trees or on field between cropping season to protect the land from leaching and erosion:

choiceExplanations.Catch crop: Fast-growing secondary crop planted to utilize residual moisture or replace a failed main crop for harvest.
choiceExplanations.Nurse crop: Companion crop grown to shelter or support a slower-establishing main crop rather than protect bare soil between seasons.
choiceExplanations.Cover crop: Correct — A cover crop shields bare soil between orchard rows or cropping seasons against raindrop impact, erosion, and nutrient leaching.
choiceExplanations.Trap crop: Sacrificial plant grown to attract pests away from a primary cash crop.

items.question: A practical adaptation of reforestation whereby the species planted have economic value, such as mango, pili and so on.

choiceExplanations.Silviculture: General practice of cultivating and managing forest trees primarily for timber production.
choiceExplanations.Agroforestry: Correct — Agroforestry integrates high-value fruit or tree crops like mango and pili into land rehabilitation for ecological and economic returns.
choiceExplanations.Afforestation: Establishing a forest on land that previously lacked tree cover, not specifically using economic orchard species.
choiceExplanations.Silvopasture: Combining forestry trees with forage and grazing livestock on the same land unit.

items.question: Is soil detachment and transport resulting from the impact of water drops directly on soil particles or on thin water surfaces.

choiceExplanations.Splash raindrop erosion: Correct — Splash raindrop erosion is the detachment and scattering of soil particles caused directly by falling raindrops on soil or thin water films.
choiceExplanations.Gully erosion: Deep, advanced channel erosion formed by concentrated runoff rather than direct raindrop impact.
choiceExplanations.Sheet erosion: Uniform removal of thin soil layers across a surface by shallow overland flow.
choiceExplanations.Rill erosion: Cutting of small, shallow channels by concentrated surface runoff down a slope.

items.question: Land slides and slips due to saturation of steep hills and slopes.

choiceExplanations.Gully erosions: Incision of deep channels by concentrated surface runoff rather than mass slope failure.
choiceExplanations.Sheet erosions: Gradual uniform removal of thin topsoil layers by shallow overland flow.
choiceExplanations.Streambank erosions: Scouring of river and creek banks by flowing channel water.
choiceExplanations.Slip erosions: Correct — Slip erosion refers to mass downslope movement such as landslides and earth slips triggered when steep saturated slopes lose shear strength.

items.question: Erosion caused by wave action on the seashore.

choiceExplanations.Gully erosions: Deep upland channel erosion formed by concentrated rainfall runoff rather than ocean waves.
choiceExplanations.Slip erosions: Mass sliding of saturated hillsides rather than marine shoreline erosion.
choiceExplanations.Streambank erosions: Erosion along river and stream banks caused by unidirectional channel flow.
choiceExplanations.Coastal erosions: Correct — Coastal erosion is the wearing away of shorelines and beaches by ocean wave action, tides, and currents.

items.question: Is the detachment and transport of soil particles from the land by water or wind action.

choiceExplanations.Soil compaction: Compression of soil pores under load, increasing bulk density without transporting particles off-site.
choiceExplanations.Soil deposition: Settling or dropping of eroded sediment onto lower terrain rather than detachment and removal.
choiceExplanations.Soil erosion: Correct — Soil erosion is the detachment and transport of soil particles from land surfaces by water or wind.
choiceExplanations.Soil subsidence: Gradual sinking of the land surface due to subsurface consolidation or groundwater withdrawal.

items.question: Vulnerability or susceptibility of the soil to erosion. It is a function of both the physical properties of the soil and land management practices.

choiceExplanations.Infiltrability: Rate or capacity at which water enters the soil surface, not susceptibility to erosion.
choiceExplanations.Erodibility: Correct — Erodibility is a soil's inherent vulnerability to detachment and transport, governed by physical soil properties and management.
choiceExplanations.Permeability: Ease with which water or air transmits through connected soil pores.
choiceExplanations.Erosivity: Potential ability of rainfall or wind energy to cause erosion, rather than the soil's own susceptibility.

items.question: Moisture content present in the soil when gravitational water has been removed is called:

choiceExplanations.Permanent wilting point: Lower soil moisture threshold around 15 atm tension at which plants cannot recover from wilting.
choiceExplanations.Hygroscopic coefficient: Tightly bound adsorbed moisture film at roughly 31 atm unavailable to plant roots.
choiceExplanations.Saturation point: Maximum water content when all soil voids are completely filled with water.
choiceExplanations.Field capacity: Correct — Field capacity is the soil moisture remaining after free gravitational water has drained from macropores.

items.question: The mass per unit volume of the soil particles is:

choiceExplanations.Void ratio: Ratio of pore volume to solid particle volume, not mass per unit volume.
choiceExplanations.Porosity: Correct — Keyed as the intended answer in the reviewer, though porosity is strictly pore-to-total volume while particle density is particle mass per unit volume.
choiceExplanations.Permeability: Measure of how readily fluid flows through porous soil under a hydraulic gradient.
choiceExplanations.Bulk density: Mass of dry soil solids divided by total bulk soil volume including pores.

items.question: The ratio of the volume of pores to the volume of solid is:

choiceExplanations.Degree of saturation: Ratio of water volume to total pore volume expressed as a fraction or percentage.
choiceExplanations.Porosity: Ratio of pore volume to total soil bulk volume rather than solid volume.
choiceExplanations.Void ratio: Correct — Void ratio (e = Vv / Vs) is defined as the volume of void spaces divided by the volume of solid particles.
choiceExplanations.Specific retention: Ratio of water volume retained against gravity to the total bulk soil volume.

items.question: Water held by forces of surface tension and continuous films around the soil particles is:

choiceExplanations.Gravitational water: Free-draining water in macropores that moves downward primarily under gravity.
choiceExplanations.Structural water: Chemically bound water forming part of soil mineral crystal structures, removable only by intense heating.
choiceExplanations.Hygroscopic water: Tightly adsorbed thin film on particle surfaces held at ~31 atm and unavailable to plants.
choiceExplanations.Capillary water: Correct — Capillary water is held in micropores as continuous films around soil particles by surface tension and cohesion forces.

items.question: Water held tightly to the surface of soil particle by adsorption forces is:

choiceExplanations.Capillary water: Available water held in small pores by surface tension forces rather than tight surface adsorption.
choiceExplanations.Hygroscopic water: Correct — Hygroscopic water is held tightly as an extremely thin film around soil particles by strong adsorption forces.
choiceExplanations.Gravitational water: Free water in large pores that drains downward rapidly under gravity.
choiceExplanations.Structural water: Water chemically combined within clay mineral crystal lattices rather than surface-adsorbed moisture.

items.question: The type of erosion that takes place in small channels which cannot be obliterated by tillage operations is called

choiceExplanations.Rill: Small runoff channels shallow enough to be smoothed out by routine tillage operations.
choiceExplanations.Splash: Particle detachment caused by direct impact of falling raindrops on bare soil.
choiceExplanations.Gully: Correct — Gully erosion cuts deep, wide channels that cannot be obliterated by normal tillage implements.
choiceExplanations.Sheet: Uniform removal of thin soil layers by shallow unchannelized overland flow.

items.question: Erosion of stream banks by flowing water.

choiceExplanations.Sheet erosion: Uniform removal of thin surface soil layers across fields by shallow overland flow.
choiceExplanations.Rill erosion: Formation of small, parallel micro-channels on sloped farmland by runoff.
choiceExplanations.Stream bank erosion: Correct — Stream bank erosion is the scouring and undercutting of river or stream channel sides by flowing water.
choiceExplanations.Gully erosion: Formation of deep upland channels in fields or hillsides rather than along natural stream banks.

items.question: A vertical section to the soil mass where significant changes in the soil texture and structure with depth are observed

choiceExplanations.Soil solum: Upper part of the soil profile comprising the A and B horizons altered by soil-forming processes, excluding parent material.
choiceExplanations.Soil profile: Correct — A soil profile is a vertical cross-section exposing all soil horizons from the surface down to parent material.
choiceExplanations.Soil monolith: Undisturbed vertical soil block extracted and preserved for display or laboratory study.
choiceExplanations.Soil horizon: Single horizontal soil layer parallel to the surface with distinct properties, rather than the entire vertical sequence.

items.question: It is type of erosion where small channels are formed on the surface of the soil

choiceExplanations.Splash: Particle detachment caused by direct raindrop impact rather than flowing runoff channels.
choiceExplanations.Sheet: Uniform removal of a thin layer of topsoil without forming distinct channels.
choiceExplanations.Gully: Large, deep channels too wide and deep to be erased by ordinary tillage.
choiceExplanations.Rill: Correct — Rill erosion creates small, well-defined surface channels formed by concentrated runoff that normal tillage can still smooth out.

items.question: A property associated with surface tension of liquid and manifested in the rise and fall of liquids in small diameter tubes.

choiceExplanations.Surface viscosity: Internal resistance of a liquid surface to shearing flow, not tube rise or fall.
choiceExplanations.Hydrostatic pressure: Pressure exerted by a static fluid column due to gravity and depth alone.
choiceExplanations.Capillary action/capillarity: Correct — Capillarity is the rise or depression of liquid in small-diameter pores or tubes caused by surface tension and adhesion.
choiceExplanations.Osmotic potential: Pressure difference driven by solute concentration across a semipermeable membrane.

items.question: Water that moves freely and drains out of the soil is:

choiceExplanations.Hygroscopic: Tightly adsorbed thin moisture film that does not drain under gravity.
choiceExplanations.Capillary: Water retained in micropores by surface tension against gravitational pull.
choiceExplanations.Combined: Chemically bound water within mineral structures that cannot drain freely.
choiceExplanations.Gravitational: Correct — Gravitational water occupies macropores above field capacity and drains freely downward under gravity.

items.question: The moisture content of the soil when the tension is 1.5 atmosphere.

choiceExplanations.Hygroscopic coefficient: Moisture held tightly around soil particles at roughly 31 atmospheres of tension, unavailable to plants.
choiceExplanations.Field capacity: Soil moisture content remaining after gravitational drainage, typically occurring at about 1/3 atmosphere tension.
choiceExplanations.Permanent wilting point: Soil moisture level at 15 atmospheres tension where plants wilt and cannot recover.
choiceExplanations.Saturation point: Correct — Keyed answer in the board-reviewer source for soil moisture at the stated 1.5-atmosphere tension threshold.

items.question: Difference in moisture content of soil between field capacity and permanent wilting point.

choiceExplanations.Available moisture: Correct — Available moisture is the water held between field capacity and permanent wilting point that plant roots can extract.
choiceExplanations.Gravitational moisture: Water above field capacity that drains freely downward through macropores due to gravity.
choiceExplanations.Unavailable moisture: Water held below the permanent wilting point at tensions exceeding 15 atmospheres, unusable by plants.
choiceExplanations.Hygroscopic moisture: Thin film of water adsorbed tightly onto soil particles by molecular forces, unavailable to crops.

items.question: Small water impounding management (SWIM) projects, in general, are those small scale water impounding dams which have structural heights of not more than.

choiceExplanations.35 m: Exceeds the Philippine SWIM classification limit of 30 m maximum structural dam height.
choiceExplanations.30 m: Correct — Under Philippine SWIM project guidelines, small-scale water impounding dams have structural heights not exceeding 30 m.
choiceExplanations.25 m: Understates the standard 30 m upper structural height limit for SWIM dams.
choiceExplanations.20 m: Below the 30 m ceiling used to classify SWIM dam heights in the Philippines.

items.question: What is the term for capillary water in the smaller pore space of the soil?

choiceExplanations.Phreatic water: Subsurface water in the saturated zone below the water table, also called groundwater.
choiceExplanations.Soil moisture: Correct — Soil moisture specifically refers to capillary water retained in the smaller unsaturated pore spaces above the water table.
choiceExplanations.Hygroscopic water: Water adsorbed as a thin film on soil grains, held too tightly for capillary flow.
choiceExplanations.Gravitational water: Free water in large pores that drains downward under gravity rather than capillary forces.

items.question: Terrace used on moderate slope (6-8%)

choiceExplanations.Conservation bench terrace: Level bench with a contributing watershed used on gentler slopes in semiarid regions.
choiceExplanations.Broad based terrace: Correct — Broad-base terraces are constructed with wide embankments and channels on gentle to moderate slopes of about 6–8%.
choiceExplanations.Narrow based terrace: Embankment terrace with steep, uncultivated sides typically applied on steeper slopes than broad-base terraces.
choiceExplanations.Bench terrace: Step-like terrace cut into steep slopes (typically 15–30% or more) for intensive cultivation.

items.question: In Earth embankment, on structures less than 15 m high with average materials, the side slopes should be steeper than_____on the upstream face

choiceExplanations.3:1: Correct — Standard earth embankment design for structures under 15 m uses a 3:1 (H:V) upstream slope limit for stability.
choiceExplanations.4:1: Flatter than the standard 3:1 upstream slope specification for embankments under 15 m high.
choiceExplanations.4:2: Equivalent to a 2:1 ratio, which is too steep for the saturated upstream face.
choiceExplanations.2:1: Typical minimum slope for the downstream face rather than the upstream face.

items.question: In Earth embankment, on structures less than 15 m high with average materials, the side slopes should be steeper than_____on the downstream face

choiceExplanations.1:1: Excessively steep for an earth embankment, risking slope failure and sloughing.
choiceExplanations.2:1: Correct — Standard design specifies a 2:1 (H:V) side slope limit on the downstream face of small earth embankments under 15 m.
choiceExplanations.3:1: Standard slope ratio prescribed for the upstream face rather than the downstream face.
choiceExplanations.3:2: Equivalent to 1.5:1, which is steeper than the standard 2:1 downstream embankment slope.

items.question: Measure Specific Gravity

choiceExplanations.Hydrometer: Correct — A hydrometer measures the specific gravity (relative density) of liquids or soil-water suspensions by buoyancy.
choiceExplanations.Permeameter: Measures hydraulic conductivity (permeability) of soil samples rather than specific gravity.
choiceExplanations.Hygrometer: Measures atmospheric relative humidity or moisture content in air.
choiceExplanations.Tensiometer: Measures soil water matric potential (tension) in the field.

items.question: SMALL WATER IMPOUNDING SYSTEM: Height

choiceExplanations.15–25m: Exceeds the typical 5–15 m dam height range specified for Philippine SWIS projects.
choiceExplanations.10–20m: Shifts above the standard 5–15 m height range for SWIS embankments.
choiceExplanations.5-15m: Correct — Small Water Impounding Systems (SWIS) under DA-BSWM standards typically have embankment heights of 5–15 m.
choiceExplanations.25–35m: Corresponds to larger dams exceeding standard SWIS and even typical SWIM height bounds.

items.question: SWIS: Service area

choiceExplanations.88–212 ha: Does not match the standard 25–150 ha SWIS irrigable service area guideline.
choiceExplanations.150–275 ha: Exceeds the typical 25–150 ha service area range of a SWIS project.
choiceExplanations.275–400 ha: Falls within larger communal or national irrigation ranges, beyond SWIS capacity.
choiceExplanations.25-150 ha: Correct — Under Philippine SWIS design criteria, the typical irrigable service area is 25–150 hectares.

items.question: SWIS: Upstream Face(inside slope)

choiceExplanations.2.48:1: Steeper than the standard 2.75:1 SWIS upstream slope specification.
choiceExplanations.2.20:1: Too steep for the upstream face, which faces saturation and drawdown stresses.
choiceExplanations.2.75:1: Correct — PAES / BSWM design standards for SWIS specify a 2.75:1 (H:V) slope on the upstream inside face.
choiceExplanations.3.03:1: Flatter than the standard 2.75:1 SWIS upstream face slope ratio.

items.question: SWIS: Downstream Face(outside slope)

choiceExplanations.2.00:1: Steeper than the 2.50:1 downstream slope specified in SWIS embankment standards.
choiceExplanations.2.50:1: Correct — SWIS embankment standards specify a 2.50:1 (H:V) slope on the downstream outside face.
choiceExplanations.2.25:1: Slightly steeper than the standard 2.50:1 SWIS downstream slope criterion.
choiceExplanations.2.75:1: Standard slope ratio for the SWIS upstream face, not the downstream face.

items.question: SWIS: soil type

choiceExplanations.atleast 35% clay: Higher than the minimum 30% clay content required for SWIS embankment soil.
choiceExplanations.atleast 30% clay: Correct — SWIS earthfill construction requires soil containing at least 30% clay to ensure low permeability and stability.
choiceExplanations.atleast 25% clay: Below the 30% minimum clay fraction needed for an impervious SWIS embankment.
choiceExplanations.atleast 20% clay: Insufficient clay content to prevent excessive seepage in a SWIS earth dam.

items.question: A thin film of soil layer detached and transported by water flowing on the land surface

choiceExplanations.Sheet erosion: Correct — Sheet erosion is the uniform removal of a thin layer of topsoil across a surface by overland sheet flow.
choiceExplanations.Splash erosion: Detachment of soil particles caused directly by raindrop impact rather than surface flow.
choiceExplanations.Rill erosion: Soil removal concentrated in small, well-defined channels that can still be obliterated by tillage.
choiceExplanations.Gully erosion: Advanced erosion carving deep channels too large to be crossed or smoothed by farm machinery.

items.question: What is the typical soil moisture tension at field capacity?
items.rationale: Field capacity occurs at a soil moisture tension of about 1/3 atm (0.33 bar) after excess gravitational water drains, whereas permanent wilting point is at 15 atm and the hygroscopic coefficient is about 31 atm.

choiceExplanations.15 atm: Typical soil moisture tension at the permanent wilting point, not field capacity.
choiceExplanations.1/3 atm: Correct — Field capacity is commonly defined at a matric tension of about 1/3 atmosphere (33 kPa).
choiceExplanations.Coastal erosions: An erosion process along shorelines, unrelated to soil moisture tension.
choiceExplanations.31 atm: Approximate tension at the hygroscopic coefficient, far drier than field capacity.

items.question: is the ratio of the pore volume to the total bulk volume of the soil

choiceExplanations.Bulk density: Ratio of oven-dry soil mass to total bulk volume, not pore volume.
choiceExplanations.Void ratio: Ratio of pore volume to the volume of solid soil particles alone.
choiceExplanations.Soil porosity: Correct — Soil porosity (n) is defined as the ratio of pore volume to total bulk soil volume.
choiceExplanations.Particle density: Ratio of solid soil mass to the volume of solid particles only.

items.question: is the ratio of the pore volume to the volume of the soil

choiceExplanations.Specific gravity: Ratio of a material's density to the density of water at a reference temperature.
choiceExplanations.Soil porosity: Ratio of pore volume to the total bulk volume of the soil.
choiceExplanations.Bulk density: Mass of dry soil solids divided by total bulk soil volume.
choiceExplanations.Void ratio: Correct — Void ratio (e) is the ratio of the volume of voids (pores) to the volume of soil solids.

items.question: overflow structure built across a river to raise the upstream water level in order to facilitate the water diversion into the main canal by gravity

choiceExplanations.Sluice gate: Movable gate controlling flow through an opening or flushing sediment, not an overflow river weir.
choiceExplanations.Check dam: Small barrier built across gullies or channels primarily to trap sediment and slow erosion.
choiceExplanations.Storage dam: Large dam designed primarily to impound significant water volume in a reservoir over time.
choiceExplanations.Diversion dam: Correct — A diversion dam (or weir) raises river water stage to divert water by gravity into an irrigation canal.

items.question: hydraulic structure that dissipates energy and connect mildly sloping irrigation canals built along a steeply sloping land

choiceExplanations.Drop fall structure: Correct — A drop structure lowers canal water from a higher to a lower level while dissipating excess kinetic energy.
choiceExplanations.Inverted siphon: Closed conduit carrying canal water under pressure beneath roads, drains, or depressions.
choiceExplanations.Check structure: Gate or weir inside a canal used to maintain upstream water level for turnout delivery.
choiceExplanations.Division box: Structure that splits irrigation flow proportionately into two or more distribution ditches.

items.question: Used for 25-30%

choiceExplanations.Broad-Base Terrace: Farmable embankment terrace suited only for gentle to moderate slopes up to about 8%.
choiceExplanations.Bench Terrace: Correct — Bench terraces convert steep hillsides of around 25–30% slope into flat or nearly flat cultivated steps.
choiceExplanations.Zingg Terrace: Conservation bench terrace typically recommended on moderate slopes below 25%.
choiceExplanations.Graded Terrace: Channel terrace sloped gently along its contour to drain runoff slowly on mild-to-moderate slopes.

items.question: Type of terrace that is used for 9-24% slope.

choiceExplanations.Zing or conservation: Correct — Zingg (conservation bench) terraces are commonly recommended in ABELE review materials for slopes of 9–24%.
choiceExplanations.Broad-based or ridge: Used on gentler slopes (generally below 8–10%) where machinery can farm over the ridge.
choiceExplanations.Bench or step: Constructed on steeper slopes (typically 25–30% and above) as leveled agricultural benches.
choiceExplanations.Diversion or graded: Channel terraces designed to intercept and convey excess runoff across gentler slopes.

items.question: RAINWATER & RUNOFF MANAGEMENT: Depth of diversion channel in SFR – Small Farm Reservoir

choiceExplanations.0.92m: Deeper than the standard 0.75 m diversion channel depth specified for Small Farm Reservoirs.
choiceExplanations.0.66m: Shallower than the 0.75 m design depth of an SFR diversion channel.
choiceExplanations.0.75m: Correct — PAES / BSWM Small Farm Reservoir guidelines specify a standard diversion channel depth of 0.75 m.
choiceExplanations.0.86m: Exceeds the standard 0.75 m depth criterion for an SFR diversion channel.

items.question: small farm reservoir height

choiceExplanations.4m: Below the 5 m maximum embankment height defining a Small Farm Reservoir.
choiceExplanations.5m: Correct — Small Farm Reservoirs (SFR) are low-embankment earth structures with heights not exceeding 5 m.
choiceExplanations.6m: Exceeds the 5 m maximum structural height limit of a Small Farm Reservoir.
choiceExplanations.7m: Falls above the 5 m ceiling, placing it into the SWIS height range.

items.question: Ratio of the bulk density of the soil with the density of water

choiceExplanations.Dry bulk density: Oven-dry mass of soil divided by total bulk volume, expressed in mass per volume units.
choiceExplanations.Apparent SG: Correct — Apparent specific gravity (As) equals soil bulk density divided by the density of water.
choiceExplanations.Particle density: Mass of solid soil particles divided by the volume of those solids alone.
choiceExplanations.Real SG: Ratio of soil particle density (excluding pore spaces) to the density of water.

items.question: Bulk density of rice husk

choiceExplanations.100-120kg: Correct — Loose rice husk has a standard bulk density of approximately 100–120 kg/m³.
choiceExplanations.120–140kg: Slightly higher than the standard 100–120 kg/m³ bulk density of uncompacted rice husk.
choiceExplanations.140–160kg: Overestimates the bulk density of loose rice husk unless compacted or ground.
choiceExplanations.80–100kg: Underestimates the typical 100–120 kg/m³ bulk density value used for rice husk.

items.question: Bulk density of rice paddy

choiceExplanations.662kg: Higher than the standard ~576 kg/m³ bulk density of rough rice (paddy).
choiceExplanations.576kg: Correct — Rough rice (paddy) has a standard bulk density of approximately 576 kg/m³ (about 36 lb/ft³).
choiceExplanations.507kg: Underestimates the standard 576 kg/m³ bulk density of paddy rice.
choiceExplanations.622kg: Exceeds the standard reference bulk density of 576 kg/m³ for paddy.

items.question: bulk density of corn

choiceExplanations.720 kg: Correct — Shelled corn has a standard bulk density of approximately 720 kg/m³ (about 45 lb/ft³).
choiceExplanations.576 kg: Standard bulk density of rough rice (paddy), not shelled corn.
choiceExplanations.662 kg: Lower than the standard 720 kg/m³ bulk density for shelled corn.
choiceExplanations.778 kg: Closer to the bulk density of wheat or denser grains rather than corn.

items.question: Bulk density of rice rusks.

choiceExplanations.80–100 kg/m3: Slightly below the standard 100–120 kg/m³ bulk density range for rice husks.
choiceExplanations.120–140 kg/m3: Exceeds the standard 100–120 kg/m³ bulk density of loose rice husks.
choiceExplanations.140–160 kg/m3: Overestimates loose rice husk bulk density, representing compacted material instead.
choiceExplanations.100-120 kg/m3: Correct — Loose rice husks typically have a bulk density of 100–120 kg/m³.

items.question: It is the water retained about individual soil particles by molecular action and can be removed only by heating

choiceExplanations.Hygroscopic water: Correct — Hygroscopic water adheres tightly to soil particles by molecular attraction and requires oven heating to remove.
choiceExplanations.Capillary water: Water held in micropores by surface tension, extractable by plant roots.
choiceExplanations.Available water: Soil moisture between field capacity and permanent wilting point usable by plants.
choiceExplanations.Gravitational water: Free water in macropores that drains downward by gravity without heating.

items.question: The aggregation of soil particles into peds.

choiceExplanations.Soil consistency: Behavior of soil under mechanical stress across dry, moist, and wet states.
choiceExplanations.Soil structure: Correct — Soil structure is the arrangement and aggregation of primary sand, silt, and clay particles into peds.
choiceExplanations.Soil texture: Relative proportions of sand, silt, and clay particles in a soil.
choiceExplanations.Soil porosity: Fraction of total soil volume occupied by air- or water-filled pores.

items.question: Determine the soil moisture content in both dry and wet bases, respectively, if the wet soil is 91 g and the dry soil after oven drying is 77 g.
items.rationale: Weight of water = 91 - 77 = 14 g; dry-basis moisture content = (14 / 77) × 100% = 18.18% (≈ 18%), and wet-basis moisture content = (14 / 91) × 100% = 15.38% (≈ 15%).

choiceExplanations.20%, 17%: Incorrect ratios; 14 g of water divided by 77 g and 91 g yields 18% and 15%.
choiceExplanations.19%, 16%: Slightly overestimates both the dry-basis (18.2%) and wet-basis (15.4%) moisture percentages.
choiceExplanations.18%, 15%: Correct — With 14 g of water (91 − 77 g), dry-basis moisture is 14/77 ≈ 18% and wet-basis moisture is 14/91 ≈ 15%.
choiceExplanations.21%, 18%: Overstates both moisture contents for 14 g of water in 77 g dry / 91 g wet soil.

items.question: Which one is not a type of commonly used on-farm reservoir?
items.rationale: Per PAES 610:2016 (Small Farm Reservoir), the standard on-farm reservoir types are dugout pond, regular balanced excavation (not irregular), semicircular embankment, and straight embankment.

choiceExplanations.Dugout pond: Common on-farm reservoir excavated below ground level on flat terrain.
choiceExplanations.Straight embankment: Common on-farm reservoir built by placing a straight dam across a gentle depression or valley.
choiceExplanations.Irregular balanced excavation: Correct — Irregular balanced excavation is not a standard on-farm reservoir type (unlike dugout, straight, and semicircular embankments).
choiceExplanations.Semicircular embankment: Standard on-farm reservoir design using a curved dike on gentle slopes to impound runoff.

items.question: In comparing sites for a straight embankment type small farm reservoir project, the suitable slope is ____ %.
items.rationale: Per PAES 610:2016 (Small Farm Reservoir, Table 1), the suitable terrain slope range for a straight embankment type small farm reservoir is 2–15%.

choiceExplanations.3-10: Narrower than the standard 2–15% suitable slope range for a straight embankment SFR.
choiceExplanations.5-20: Upper bound of 20% is too steep for economical straight-embankment SFR siting.
choiceExplanations.5-15: Excludes gentler 2–5% slopes that are still suitable for straight-embankment SFRs.
choiceExplanations.2-15: Correct — Straight-embankment Small Farm Reservoirs are typically sited on gently sloping to undulating terrain of 2–15%.

items.question: This forms dense mat on the bottom of ponds and serves as food of young milkfishes.

choiceExplanations.Azolla: Floating aquatic fern used as biofertilizer or supplemental feed, not a benthic mat.
choiceExplanations.Lumut: Filamentous green algae favored by older milkfish rather than young fry or fingerlings.
choiceExplanations.Plankton: Microscopic suspended organisms in the water column rather than a dense bottom mat.
choiceExplanations.Lab-lab: Correct — Lab-lab is a benthic biological complex of algae, bacteria, and microfauna forming a bottom mat eaten by young milkfish.

items.question: water containing less than 500 ppm dissolved common salt, sodium chloride, such as that in groundwater, rivers, ponds, and lakes

choiceExplanations.Seawater: Marine water with high salinity, typically around 35,000 ppm (35 ppt) dissolved salts.
choiceExplanations.Freshwater: Correct — Freshwater is defined in PAES aquaculture standards as water containing less than 500 ppm dissolved sodium chloride.
choiceExplanations.Hypersaline: Water whose salinity exceeds normal seawater (>35–40 ppt), such as brine ponds.
choiceExplanations.Brackishwater: Mixture of freshwater and seawater with salinity between about 0.5 ppt and 30 ppt.

items.question: Using your knowledge in pumps, which of the following pumps is best for pumping water with algae from a 5.6-cubic meter hatchery tank into a series of milkfish larval rearing tanks?

choiceExplanations.Centrifugal pump: Surface-mounted centrifugal pump requires priming and is less convenient for direct tank transfer here.
choiceExplanations.Turbine pump: Deep-well multi-stage pump designed for high-head groundwater extraction, not shallow hatchery tanks.
choiceExplanations.Reciprocating pump: Positive-displacement piston pump unsuited for gentle transfer of fragile algae-laden hatchery water.
choiceExplanations.Submersible pump: Correct — A submersible pump operates directly inside the hatchery tank without priming, efficiently transferring algae-rich water to larval tanks.

items.question: Which pump is appropriate for pumping muddy water from a tilapia fish pond?

choiceExplanations.Submersible pump: Standard clean-water submersible pumps risk impeller clogging or abrasion when handling heavy pond mud.
choiceExplanations.Reciprocating pump: Correct — In ABELE aquaculture questions, a reciprocating positive-displacement pump is selected for handling viscous or muddy pond water.
choiceExplanations.Turbine pump: Precision multi-stage well pump easily damaged by suspended mud and silt.
choiceExplanations.Jet pump: Relies on a small nozzle/venturi that clogs rapidly in muddy water.

items.question: Examine the aquaculture engineering requirements of high value tropical fishes. From the ancillary structures enumerated below, what is not needed for milkfish?

choiceExplanations.Breeder conditioning tank: Correct — Milkfish hatcheries require algal, rotifer, and larval rearing tanks, whereas breeder conditioning tanks are typically used for tilapia or catfish.
choiceExplanations.Algal tank: Essential in milkfish hatcheries to culture microalgae that feed rotifers and condition larval water.
choiceExplanations.Rotifer tank: Essential live-feed culture tank producing Brachionus rotifers for newly hatched milkfish larvae.
choiceExplanations.Larval rearing tank: Core hatchery tank where fertilized milkfish eggs hatch and larvae grow.

items.question: Considering the milkfish ancillary structures enumerated below, what is the most costly in terms of materials and labor per unit volume?

choiceExplanations.Rotifer tank: Smaller, shallower live-feed tank with lower structural wall thickness and cost per unit volume.
choiceExplanations.Broodstock tank: Correct — Milkfish broodstock tanks are large, deep, heavily reinforced circular concrete structures, making them the most expensive per unit volume.
choiceExplanations.Larval rearing tank: Smaller than broodstock tanks and requires lighter structural reinforcement.
choiceExplanations.Algal tank: Shallow culture tank with relatively minimal structural reinforcement costs.

items.question: Based on the environmental requirements of milkfish or bangus (Chanos chanos), it can be grown in _______ water.

choiceExplanations.Both marine and fresh: Correct — Milkfish are euryhaline and can be cultured across freshwater, brackishwater, and marine environments.
choiceExplanations.Only fresh: Incorrect because milkfish naturally spawn in marine waters and thrive in brackish or marine ponds.
choiceExplanations.Only brackish: Incorrect because milkfish also grow well in freshwater lakes and marine cages.
choiceExplanations.Only marine: Incorrect because milkfish are widely cultured in brackishwater fishponds and freshwater pens.

items.question: Considering the water salinity requirements of milkfish, it can thrive in salinity level of _______.

choiceExplanations.120-160 ppt: Extreme hypersaline concentration far beyond the osmotic tolerance of milkfish.
choiceExplanations.40-80 ppt: Hypersaline range exceeding normal marine salinity and stressful or lethal to milkfish.
choiceExplanations.0-40 ppt: Correct — Milkfish are euryhaline fish that tolerate and thrive across salinities from 0 to 40 ppt.
choiceExplanations.80-120 ppt: Extremely hypersaline water incapable of supporting milkfish growth or survival.

items.question: Considering the BFAR standard, the intensive stocking density of growing tilapia should be ___ heads per square meter.

choiceExplanations.>6: Below the >8 heads/m² BFAR threshold distinguishing intensive tilapia culture.
choiceExplanations.>7: Understates the >8 heads/m² minimum stocking density for intensive tilapia farming.
choiceExplanations.>9: Higher than the >8 heads/m² baseline set by BFAR for intensive stocking.
choiceExplanations.>8: Correct — Under BFAR / PAES standards, intensive tilapia culture uses stocking densities greater than 8 heads per square meter.

items.question: Applying the BFAR recommended practice, what is the minimum age of tilapia fry at time of disposal?

choiceExplanations.23 days: Exceeds the standard 21-day minimum age recommended for tilapia fry disposal.
choiceExplanations.21 days: Correct — BFAR recommends disposing or stocking tilapia fry at a minimum age of 21 days (about 3 weeks).
choiceExplanations.27 days: Nearly four weeks old, beyond the 21-day minimum disposal age.
choiceExplanations.18 days: Too young and fragile compared with BFAR's 21-day minimum disposal standard.

items.question: In aquaculture engineering, the horizontal cross-section of a milkfish broodstock tank is normally of ________ shape.

choiceExplanations.Rectangular: Causes corners where large milkfish broodstock can injure themselves or experience poor circulation.
choiceExplanations.Square: Corners disrupt continuous circular swimming and self-cleaning hydraulic flow.
choiceExplanations.Circular: Correct — Circular tanks support continuous swimming without sharp corners and provide uniform self-cleaning radial water flow for milkfish broodstock.
choiceExplanations.Octagonal: Creates angled walls and eddies, unlike standard circular milkfish broodstock tanks.

items.question: In the practice of aquaculture engineering, the horizontal cross-section of a catfish larval rearing tank is normally of ________ shape.

choiceExplanations.Square or rectangular: Correct — Catfish larval rearing tanks are commonly square or rectangular for efficient hatchery space utilization and easy grading.
choiceExplanations.Circular or cylindrical: Standard for pelagic swimmers like milkfish broodstock rather than benthic catfish larvae.
choiceExplanations.Triangular or trapezoidal: Uncommon geometry in aquaculture tanks with awkward corners and poor flow distribution.
choiceExplanations.Hexagonal or octagonal: Rarely used for catfish larval tanks due to higher formwork and layout costs.

items.question: In the design of milkfish and tilapia larval rearing tanks, the ______ is made of a partially transparent material.

choiceExplanations.Floor: Built of solid concrete or lined base to support water weight and prevent leakage.
choiceExplanations.Partition: Internal dividing wall rather than a light-transmitting overhead cover.
choiceExplanations.Roof: Correct — A partially transparent roof lets in controlled sunlight for algal growth and temperature regulation while sheltering tanks from rain.
choiceExplanations.Wall: Usually constructed of opaque concrete or masonry to retain water pressure safely.

items.question: Per BFAR standard, the intensive stocking density of tilapia is __ heads per square meter.

choiceExplanations.>9: Overstates the >8 heads/m² BFAR cutoff for intensive tilapia stocking density.
choiceExplanations.>8: Correct — BFAR classifies intensive tilapia culture as having a stocking density greater than 8 heads/m².
choiceExplanations.>7: Falls short of the >8 heads/m² threshold defined for intensive tilapia production.
choiceExplanations.>6: Represents semi-intensive rather than intensive tilapia stocking under BFAR standards.

items.question: Intensive fish stocking density needs _________ feeds.

choiceExplanations.Natural: Pond plankton or benthic organisms alone cannot sustain high-density intensive fish populations.
choiceExplanations.Organic: Refers to certification or ingredient sourcing rather than the complete-diet requirement of intensive culture.
choiceExplanations.Commercial: Correct — Intensive aquaculture relies on nutritionally complete commercial formulated feeds because natural pond food is insufficient at high densities.
choiceExplanations.Supplemental: Partial feeding used in semi-intensive ponds where natural food still supplies most nutrients.

items.question: Tilapia fingerlings daily need feeds equivalent to ____% of body weight.

choiceExplanations.0-15: Correct — Keyed BFAR feeding-rate range (representing up to 15% of body weight daily, commonly 10–15% for tilapia fingerlings).
choiceExplanations.6-16: Does not match the standard tilapia fingerling daily feeding rate range in BFAR tables.
choiceExplanations.4-13: Lower upper bound than the standard 15% peak daily feeding rate for fingerlings.
choiceExplanations.5-14: Slight mismatch with the standard 15% maximum fingerling feeding rate.

items.question: Tilapia feeding frequency.

choiceExplanations.6-7 times daily: Excessively frequent for grow-out tilapia, increasing labor and feed wastage.
choiceExplanations.2-3 times daily: Correct — Standard BFAR practice feeds growing tilapia 2–3 times daily for efficient intake and water quality management.
choiceExplanations.0-1 times daily: Insufficient frequency for optimal growth and feed conversion in cultured tilapia.
choiceExplanations.4-5 times daily: Typically reserved for very small fry rather than standard grow-out tilapia feeding.

items.question: A marketable size tilapia weighs ___ grams/head.

choiceExplanations.>82: Fish around 82 grams per head are still sub-marketable fingerling-to-growout stock below the standard harvest threshold.
choiceExplanations.>100: Although 100 grams is a common retail size, this standard cites over 91 grams as the minimum marketable weight.
choiceExplanations.>91: Correct — Philippine aquaculture standards define marketable-size tilapia as weighing more than 91 grams per head.
choiceExplanations.>73: Tilapia weighing 73 grams per head are still undersized juveniles requiring additional grow-out feeding before harvest.

items.question: Tilapia fry daily needs feeds equivalent to ____% of body weight.

choiceExplanations.13-26: This range underestimates the high metabolic feeding rate required by fast-growing tilapia fry.
choiceExplanations.16-33: This range slightly overstates the standard daily feeding percentage recommended for tilapia fry.
choiceExplanations.15-30: Correct — Tilapia fry require a high daily feeding rate equal to 15–30% of their body weight.
choiceExplanations.14-28: This narrower percentage bracket does not match the standard 15–30% feeding rate for tilapia fry.

items.question: If tilapia stocking relies only on natural food source, how many tilapia fingerlings should be stocked in each of 50 experimental cages, each cage has a diameter of 1 meter and depth of 1 meter? Mortality safety factor is 7% for small cages.
items.answer: Tilapia extensive stocking density (relies only on natural food source): 3 heads/m2
items.rationale: Tilapia extensive stocking density (relies only on natural food source): 3 heads/m2 / Area of cage = 3.14 (1 m)2/4 = 0.785 m2 / Stocks = Density x Area x (1+ safety factor) / = 3 x 0.785 x (1.07) / = 3 heads/cage
choices: Tilapia semi-intensive stocking density (uses natural and supplemental food): 10 heads per square meter
Tilapia intensive stocking density (relies purely on commercial feeds): 25 heads per square meter
Tilapia extensive stocking density (relies only on natural food source): 3 heads/m2
Tilapia super-intensive stocking density (requires continuous mechanical aeration): 50 heads per square meter

choiceExplanations.Tilapia semi-intensive stocking density: Semi-intensive culture supplements natural food with extra feeds, rather than relying solely on natural food.
choiceExplanations.Tilapia intensive stocking density (reli: Intensive culture relies heavily on commercial feeds at high density, not solely on natural food.
choiceExplanations.Tilapia extensive stocking density (reli: Correct — Extensive culture relies exclusively on natural food, corresponding to a stocking density of 3 heads/m2.
choiceExplanations.Tilapia super-intensive stocking density: Super-intensive culture depends on complete commercial feeds and continuous aeration, unsuitable for natural-food-only systems.

items.question: This shrimp or prawn undergoes 11 larval stages to metamorphose to post larvae:

choiceExplanations.Pacific white shrimp: Pacific white shrimp (*Litopenaeus vannamei*) passes through nauplius, protozoea, and mysis substages rather than 11 zoeal stages.
choiceExplanations.Giant tiger prawn: Giant tiger prawn (*Penaeus monodon*) develops through nauplius, protozoea, and mysis stages instead of 11 larval stages.
choiceExplanations.Indian white prawn: Indian white prawn (*Fenneropenaeus indicus*) follows the penaeid nauplius-protozoea-mysis sequence rather than 11 larval stages.
choiceExplanations.Giant freshwater prawn: Correct — The giant freshwater prawn (*Macrobrachium rosenbergii*) undergoes 11 distinct larval stages before becoming post-larvae.

items.question: Breeding and growout production of commercially important marine species are grown in zonified marine cages which the Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources refers to as:

choiceExplanations.Marine reserves: Marine reserves are protected coastal areas managed for biodiversity conservation and regulated fishing, not cage farming.
choiceExplanations.Fish sanctuaries: Fish sanctuaries are strict no-take zones dedicated to fish spawning and stock recovery rather than commercial growout.
choiceExplanations.Mariculture parks: Correct — BFAR designates zonified marine cage production areas for breeding and growout as mariculture parks.
choiceExplanations.Aquaculture zones: Aquaculture zones is a general zoning term rather than BFAR's specific program name for marine cage parks.

items.question: The rearing of fishes at ocean is referred as ______

choiceExplanations.Polyculture: Polyculture is the simultaneous farming of two or more compatible aquatic species in the same water body.
choiceExplanations.Mariculture: Correct — Mariculture is the branch of aquaculture dedicated to cultivating marine organisms in the ocean or coastal waters.
choiceExplanations.Pisciculture: Pisciculture refers broadly to fish farming in ponds, tanks, or enclosures regardless of salinity.
choiceExplanations.Monoculture: Monoculture is the cultivation of a single aquatic species within a pond, cage, or tank.

items.question: WASTE MANAGEMENT: Dissolved oxygen concentrations will be the lowest within a water body on _____

choiceExplanations.Sunrise: Correct — Overnight respiration by aquatic plants and microbes depletes oxygen continuously until photosynthesis resumes at sunrise.
choiceExplanations.Midnight: Oxygen declines at midnight, but respiration continues depleting it further throughout the remaining dark hours.
choiceExplanations.Noon: Intense midday photosynthesis actively produces oxygen, keeping dissolved oxygen levels high rather than at their minimum.
choiceExplanations.Sunset: Dissolved oxygen typically peaks around late afternoon or sunset after a full day of photosynthesis.

items.question: Estimate the inner side dimension needed in a square-shape larval rearing tank (LRT) for milkfish (Chanos chanos) if the stocking density is 25 larvae/liter and larvae stocking requirement per tank for 1 cropping batch is 25,000 larvae. The LRT has a fixed total depth of 1 m but filled at 0.7 m depth when milkfish is at larval stage.
items.rationale: Required water volume V = 25,000 / 25 = 1,000 L = 1.0 m³; at 0.7 m filled depth, base area A = 1.0 / 0.7 = 1.4286 m², giving an inner side length s = √1.4286 = 1.195 m ≈ 1.2 m.

choiceExplanations.0.21 m: A 0.21 m side yields only 0.031 m3 at 0.7 m depth, far too small for 1,000 liters.
choiceExplanations.2.1 m: A 2.1 m side holds 3,087 liters at 0.7 m depth, over three times the required 1,000-liter volume.
choiceExplanations.1.2 m: Correct — Dividing 1 m3 (25,000 / 25 L) by the 0.7 m water depth gives 1.43 m2, whose square root is 1.2 m.
choiceExplanations.Both marine and fresh: This phrase describes salinity tolerance rather than the linear tank dimension requested.

items.question: Examine the aquaculture engineering requirements of high-value tropical fishes. From the ancillary structures enumerated below, what is not needed for milkfish?
items.rationale: In a standard milkfish larval hatchery (satellite hatchery), larval rearing tanks along with algal and rotifer tanks for live-feed production are required, whereas a breeder conditioning tank is not needed.

choiceExplanations.Algal tank: Algal tanks are essential in milkfish hatcheries to culture phytoplankton as live feed for rotifers and green water.
choiceExplanations.Rotifer tank: Rotifer tanks are required to mass-produce *Brachionus* zooplankton as initial live feed for milkfish larvae.
choiceExplanations.Breeder conditional tank: Correct — Milkfish hatcheries use large broodstock tanks for spawning rather than a separate breeder conditioning tank.
choiceExplanations.Larval rearing tank: Larval rearing tanks are core hatchery units where fertilized milkfish eggs hatch and grow into fry.

items.question: Which 2 tanks should not be adjacent to each other in a marine hatchery due to danger of contamination?
items.rationale: Rotifer and algal tanks should not be adjacent because rotifers graze voraciously on microalgae; accidental transfer of rotifers into algal tanks can cause rapid algal culture crashes.

choiceExplanations.Broodstock and larval rearing tanks: Broodstock and larval tanks do not pose the severe live-feed grazing contamination risk seen between rotifers and algae.
choiceExplanations.Rotifer and algal tanks: Correct — Rotifers graze rapidly on microalgae, so placing rotifer and algal tanks adjacent risks wiping out pure algal cultures.
choiceExplanations.Broodstock and algal rearing tanks: Broodstock tanks do not rapidly consume and crash pure algal starter cultures like rotifers do.
choiceExplanations.Rotifer and broodstock tanks: Separating rotifer and broodstock tanks is less critical than isolating rotifers from pure algal culture tanks.

items.question: According to BFAR standard, the intensive stocking density of tilapia is ___ heads per square meter.
items.rationale: Per Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (BFAR) standards, tilapia pond stocking density is extensive at 1–3 heads/m², semi-intensive at 4–8 heads/m², and intensive at >8 heads/m².

choiceExplanations.>8: Correct — Under BFAR aquaculture standards, intensive tilapia culture uses stocking densities greater than 8 heads per square meter.
choiceExplanations.4-8: Stocking 4–8 heads per square meter falls within the semi-intensive tilapia culture range.
choiceExplanations.3-5: Stocking 3–5 heads per square meter corresponds to low-density extensive to lower semi-intensive management.
choiceExplanations.3: A stocking density of 3 heads per square meter represents extensive tilapia culture relying on natural food.

items.question: Which tank is the most important and most expensive in a milkfish hatchery?
items.rationale: The broodstock tank is the largest, most structurally demanding, and most expensive tank in a complete milkfish hatchery because it maintains mature spawners for continuous egg production.

choiceExplanations.Algal tank: Algal tanks are smaller auxiliary live-feed units that cost significantly less than large broodstock facilities.
choiceExplanations.Larval rearing tank: Larval rearing tanks are vital for fry production but are smaller and less expensive than broodstock tanks.
choiceExplanations.Rotifer tank: Rotifer culture tanks are secondary live-feed tanks with much lower construction costs than broodstock tanks.
choiceExplanations.Broodstock tank: Correct — The broodstock tank is the largest, most critical, and costliest facility because it houses mature spawning milkfish.

items.subtopic: 2.5 Fundamentals of Agricultural, Fishery, Ecological and Environmental Sciences
items.question: rate of evapotranspiration of a disease-free crop growing in a large field (one or more ha) under optimal soil conditions, including sufficient water and fertilizer and achieving full production potential of that crop under the given growing environment; includes water loss through transpiration by the vegetation, and vaporation from the soil surface and wet leaves

choiceExplanations.Reference evapotranspiration: Reference evapotranspiration (ETo) applies specifically to a hypothetical grass or alfalfa reference crop, not any target crop.
choiceExplanations.Actual evapotranspiration: Actual evapotranspiration (ETa) reflects real field water loss under existing, often water-stressed or suboptimal conditions.
choiceExplanations.Crop evapotranspiration: Correct — Crop evapotranspiration (ETc) is the ET of a disease-free crop under optimal soil, water, and fertility conditions.
choiceExplanations.Potential evapotranspiration: Potential evapotranspiration (PET) is a general atmospheric water-demand concept rather than FAO's specific optimal-field crop definition.

items.subtopic: 2.5 Fundamentals of Agricultural, Fishery, Ecological and Environmental Sciences
items.question: The study of the relationship among organisms and the environment in which they live, including all living and non-living components.

choiceExplanations.Pedology: Pedology is the branch of soil science focused on soil origin, morphology, classification, and mapping.
choiceExplanations.Ecology: Correct — Ecology studies the interactions between living organisms and both biotic and abiotic components of their environment.
choiceExplanations.Taxonomy: Taxonomy is the biological science of identifying, naming, and classifying organisms into hierarchical groups.
choiceExplanations.Limnology: Limnology is the specialized study of the physical, chemical, and biological properties of inland freshwaters.

items.subtopic: 2.5 Fundamentals of Agricultural, Fishery, Ecological and Environmental Sciences
items.question: This type of soil which passed through the 0.05 mm sieve but retained by the / 0.002 mm sieve.

choiceExplanations.Clay: Clay consists of soil particles smaller than 0.002 mm, which pass through the 0.002 mm boundary.
choiceExplanations.Gravel: Gravel consists of coarse mineral fragments larger than 2.0 mm, far above 0.05 mm.
choiceExplanations.Sand: Sand comprises particles between 0.05 mm and 2.0 mm, which are retained above the 0.05 mm size.
choiceExplanations.Silt: Correct — Under the USDA soil classification, silt particles measure between 0.002 mm and 0.05 mm in diameter.

items.subtopic: 2.5 Fundamentals of Agricultural, Fishery, Ecological and Environmental Sciences
items.question: 50% of the Rice Fund shall be released to and implemented by the______?

choiceExplanations.Tesda: TESDA receives 10% of the Rice Competitiveness Enhancement Fund (RCEF) for rice skills training and extension.
choiceExplanations.Landbank: Land Bank and DBP jointly manage the 10% RCEF credit facility rather than the 50% mechanization share.
